item.title: How Silence Can Erode a Relationship
item.description:
Mental Health Stigma

How Silence Can Erode a Relationship

Mental health stigma reshapes South Asian relationships.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Couples may not realize that mental health issues such as depression or ADHD are fueling recurring conflict.
  • Women tend to shoulder the burden of emotional caregiving in a relationship.
  • Family members often step in as well-intentioned but untrained mediators who may discourage seeking help.

This post is Part 2 of a series. Part 1 can be found here.

Mental health challenges rarely affect only one partner. Depression, trauma, anxiety, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), executive dysfunction, or serious mental illness often become woven into a couple's daily life and their difficulties. When stigma prevents open conversations or treatment, the relationship itself begins carrying the burden. Couples may not realize that these issues are fueling recurring conflict, leaving one partner to quietly shoulder the emotional burden.

When One Partner Carries the Relationship

Tanya Mitra is a certified life coach and founder of The REMIXED Relationship, providing culturally sensitive coaching for couples in nontraditional relationships. A cultural strategist and media expert, Mitra is featured on TLC’s "90 Day: The Hunt for Love."
Source: Tanya Mitra / Used with permission

"I often see women slowly lose themselves as emotional caretakers, a role many have been socialized to take on even without the additional responsibility of managing a partner's mental health," says Tanya Mitra, certified life coach and founder of The REMIXED Relationship. She describes women monitoring their partner's moods, anticipating triggers, and managing the emotional climate of the home. "Over time, the partnership slowly starts to feel more like caregiving than companionship. From the outside, it can look like devotion, but there's a cost."

That cost is often burnout.

When partners need support, some South Asian men struggle to recognize anxiety or depression as genuine mental health concerns rather than personality flaws, laziness, or moodiness. They may suggest tone-deaf solutions meant to motivate productivity. Others overcompensate by neglecting their own needs. Neither extreme is healthy. As Mitra explains: "One partner can gradually become the caretaker, almost like a parent figure, while the other becomes defined by their struggle. The relationship starts revolving around managing symptoms instead of nurturing connection."

Walking on Eggshells

Eventually, one partner becomes the relationship's emotional regulator, carefully choosing when or whether to raise concerns. For many South Asians, especially women, this reflects the familiar intergenerational lessons about keeping the peace.

"Over time," Mitra cautions, "You stop really knowing each other. You're no longer having hard conversations, asking deeper questions, disagreeing, dreaming, or growing together because so much energy is spent trying to avoid a reaction." Mitra calls this “the slow drift” and states, “It happens with one unsaid conversation, one avoided conflict, and one swallowed feeling at a time. Not because there's no love, but because there's very little opportunity to be genuinely yourself.”

"I learned at a very young age that I had to take care of my emotional well-being. I would hold onto feelings and explode on my partner." —Bansi, 31

Trauma often compounds these dynamics. Because many South Asians lack the language to discuss painful experiences, unresolved trauma, as in Bansi’s case, may surface after marriage, straining communication and intimacy.

Why Boundaries Feel Wrong

Deven Patel, MD, is a psychiatry resident physician at the University of California, Irvine, as well as an award-winning filmmaker and content creator. Through medicine, filmmaking, and digital media, he is passionate about using storytelling to increase awareness and reduce the stigma surrounding mental health.
Source: Deven Patel / Used with permission

Boundaries often carry negative connotations in South Asian culture. Parents may discourage locks on doors, asking for space, or prioritizing one's own needs. "It’s viewed as unkind," says Deven Patel, psychiatry resident and influencer. Mitra adds: "In many cultures, saying 'no' or prioritizing your own needs can be seen as disrespectful, selfish, or disloyal. That doesn't change the need for boundaries.” Patel adds, “We have to be able to prioritize ourselves in order to show up better for others.” What needs to change, Mitra affirms, is “how you introduce boundaries and help the people around you understand them."

Seeking Help

Culture adds another layer of complexity. Family members often step in as well-intentioned but untrained mediators, sometimes discouraging therapy altogether. In my practice, some clients hide that they are in therapy from their partners, fearing judgment or blame. Mitra has observed the same. "Some people are afraid of being seen as unstable or viewed as being 'too much' to build a future with."

Patel adds, “When we have a loved one with a mental health issue, society sometimes frames it as a ‘burden.’ But a mental health issue is no different from any other illness or physical condition.” Patel notes that older generations are often viewed as "strong" and value "powering through," while younger generations are labeled "weak." Instead, he argues, every generation has faced its own struggles. Today's youth are simply more willing to talk about them.

What Mental Health Professionals Can Do

"SA [South Asian] psychiatrists and mental health professionals can start by acknowledging the long-standing stigma that has shadowed how our communities navigate mental health," Patel says. He believes professionals must recognize that mental health conditions are too often mistaken for character flaws and have a responsibility "to unlearn damaging mindsets that we hold onto for the sake of the status quo." He also encourages clinicians to prioritize their own well-being to reduce stigma.

Despite the challenges, Patel remains hopeful. "A lot more young people are talking about mental health, going to therapy, or at least open to the idea. Social media in particular has people engaging with these concepts and talking about them more."

Ankur Varma, LCPC, is a psychotherapist, mental health advocate, and cofounder of Brown Man Therapy, a nonprofit focused on increasing dialogue and community around South Asian men's mental health.
Source: Ankur Varma / Used with permission

How Treatment Can Help

  • Shifting view of therapy: Patel encourages viewing therapy and medication no differently than treatment for any other medical condition, not as failure, but sometimes a necessity.
  • Building connection: Ankur Varma, psychotherapist and cofounder of Brown Man Therapy, emphasizes how finding support for old and new can be powerful. "The work we do in therapy centers around rebuilding those relationships and utilizing the support available to us."
  • Change is possible: Mitra reminds couples that "patterns aren't permanent. Once couples can recognize, 'This isn't just who I am, this is what I learned,' they have the opportunity to choose something different. That's where real change begins."

Mental illness does not have to determine the success or failure of a relationship. More often, secrecy, stigma, and untreated suffering quietly erode connection over time. Healing begins when couples replace silence with honest conversation, vulnerability, support, accountability, and the willingness to grow together.
